Of the antineoplastics, the greatest risk seems to be associated with alkylating agents and antimetabolites, in particular aminopterin, fluorouracil, and methotrexate.1,2,6 The vinca alkaloids and doxorubicin (but not epirubicin or idarubicin) may entail less risk,2,3 although the former have produced malformations in animals.1 Other drugs reported to be teratogenic or potentially teratogenic include bu- sulfan,1 chlorambucil,1,6 chlormethine,1 cyclophosphamide,1,6 cytarabine,1 mercaptopurine,6 and the podophyllotoxin deriva- tives.1 The problems with thalidomide and its congeners are well known. There are no specific dosage recommendations for the use of an- tineoplastics during pregnancy, but physiological changes occur- ring in the mother can alter the pharmacokinetics of drugs.1-3 This could potentially increase the toxicity of the antineoplastic, or decrease its efficacy.2 Anecdotal evidence suggests that ad- verse effects may be less marked during pregnancy, perhaps re- flecting reduced peak or free-drug concentrations in the blood.3 Myelosuppressive chemotherapy should be avoided 3 weeks be- fore the anticipated delivery so that the mother is neither neutro- penic nor thrombocytopenic.1-3 For the same reason, chemother- apy should be avoided after 35 weeks of gestation, when spontaneous delivery is more likely to occur.3 The timing of de- livery is also critical for the neonate, as chemotherapy given shortly before delivery may not be eliminated through the pla- centa, prolonging exposure in the newborn.1,3 There has also been concern that long-term occupational expo- sure to antineoplastics might have an adverse effect on the fetus of pregnant healthcare workers: a study in 650 Finnish nurses found that women who experienced fetal loss were more than twice as likely to have had first trimester exposure to antineo- plastic drugs as women who successfully gave birth.7 These re- sults have been criticised on the grounds that such results are not generally seen in cancer patients,8,9 who presumably are exposed to much higher doses of antineoplastics. However, similar results were seen in a cross-sectional analysis of 7094 pregnancies in- volving 2815 nursing and pharmacy staff.10 Another study11 has suggested that the rate of ectopic pregnancy may be increased in nurses occupationally exposed to antineoplastics, but the small number of ectopic pregnancies involved (15 in 734 pregnancies) means that the association with antineoplastics may be due to chance.
